nameStory: This little plant gets its name from Pennsylvania, where it was first scientifically described, though it actually grows throughout most of North America. The 'bittercress' part comes from its sharp, peppery taste – like many plants in the mustard family, it has a bite that makes your tongue tingle!
description: Pennsylvania bittercress is a small, delicate annual herb that belongs to the mustard family. It typically grows 6-20 inches tall with slender stems and compound leaves made up of several small leaflets. The plant produces tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in a cross pattern, which is characteristic of all mustard family plants. It's a common but often overlooked wildflower that pops up in moist, disturbed areas throughout New England.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers about 1/8 inch across with four petals arranged in a perfect cross shape. They cluster at the top of slender stems and have a fresh, slightly peppery scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves divided into 3-11 small, rounded leaflets that feel smooth and slightly succulent. The terminal (end) leaflet is usually larger than the others, creating a distinctive pattern.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Slender, upright seed pods called siliques that are about 1 inch long. When ripe, they split open explosively at the slightest touch, shooting tiny seeds several feet away.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small rosettes of leaves at the base with several branching stems rising up. The whole plant has a delicate, almost fragile appearance but is surprisingly sturdy.

idTips.label: Taste
idTips.description: Leaves and stems have a sharp, peppery bite similar to watercress or arugula. The taste is immediate and clean, without any bitter aftertaste despite the common name.

habitat: Look for Pennsylvania bittercress in moist, partially shaded areas like stream banks, wet meadows, and the edges of ponds or wetlands. It thrives in disturbed soils and is often found along trails, in gardens, or near buildings where the ground stays consistently damp. It prefers rich, organic soil and can tolerate both sun and partial shade.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin flowering in late April through May. This is the best time to spot the fresh white flowers and tender young leaves.
seasonality.summer: Continues flowering and produces explosive seed pods. The plant may look a bit scraggly in hot, dry weather but perks up after rain.
seasonality.fall: Late-season plants may still be found flowering in cool, moist spots. Seeds from spring plants germinate to create new fall rosettes.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back, but in mild winters, small rosettes may persist under snow cover in protected areas.

funFact: Pennsylvania bittercress has explosive seed pods that can launch their seeds up to 10 feet away when touched, earning it the nickname 'touch-me-not' among some botanists – try gently touching a mature seed pod and watch nature's tiny fireworks show!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with hairy bittercress, but Pennsylvania bittercress is taller, has more leaflets per leaf (usually 5-11 vs 3-7), and lacks the tiny hairs that give hairy bittercress its name. Remember: Pennsylvania = taller and smoother.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it's bitter, Pennsylvania bittercress is actually quite pleasant-tasting and edible – the 'bitter' in bittercress is somewhat misleading as it's more peppery than bitter. Many people use it as a wild green in salads or as a garnish.
compareHints: Among New England's bittercresses, Pennsylvania bittercress stands out for its smooth leaves and taller stature. Unlike the toothworts in the same genus which have thick, toothed underground stems, Pennsylvania bittercress is a surface-growing annual. It's more delicate-looking than cuckooflower and lacks the explosive spring emergence of cut-leaved toothwort.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's toothworts and bittercresses, two-leaved toothwort is unique for its simple three-parted leaves and paired leaf arrangement.
Among New England's bittercresses, hairy bittercress is distinguished by its small size, annual habit, and compound leaves with rounded leaflets.

Among its bittercress relatives, narrow-leaved bittercress stands out for its particularly slender, lance-shaped leaflets—much narrower than the rounded leaflets of hairy bittercress or the broader segments of Pennsylvania bittercress.
Among New England's toothworts, cut-leaved stands out with its three deeply-divided leaves arranged in a whorl, while two-leaved toothwort has just two broader, less-divided leaves.
Among its Cardamine relatives in New England, cuckooflower stands out for preferring wetter habitats than most bittercresses and toothworts.
Among its many Cardamine relatives in New England, bulbous cress stands out for its underground bulb and preference for very wet soils.
Among New England's bittercresses, nursery bittercress is distinguished by its completely smooth leaves and preference for disturbed garden soils.
Large toothwort differs from its close relative cut-leaved toothwort by having more finely divided, almost lacy leaflets and typically growing taller.
Among its bittercress relatives, sand bittercress is distinguished by its preference for sandy, dry soils and its particularly small size.

Alpine bittercress is dramatically different from its lowland Cardamine relatives in New England - while species like hairy bittercress and Pennsylvania bittercress are weedy annuals that pop up in gardens and disturbed areas, alpine bittercress is a specialized perennial that grows only in extreme mountain conditions.

Long's Bittercress differs from its relatives by having the most finely divided leaves in the genus - almost thread-like compared to the broader leaflets of Two-leaved Toothwort or the simpler leaves of Hairy Bittercress.

Among its Cardamine relatives in New England, Purple Cress is unique for its potential purple flower coloration - species like Two-leaved Toothwort and the various bittercresses typically stick to white or pale pink flowers.

Among the Cardamine genus in New England, white cuckoo bitter-cress has the most finely divided, feathery leaves - much more delicate than the broader leaflets of toothworts or the simpler leaves of other bitter-cresses.
Chinese Ivy differs from other Cardamine species in New England by being strictly aquatic and having a trailing, mat-forming growth habit.
